data.title: Anthropic Stock Is Finally Here. What It Means for AI, According to Dan Ives
data.description:
Until now, if you wanted to own a piece of the companies building frontier AI models, you had to buy something else first: a search giant, a cloud provider or a chipmaker. That changes this morning. Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT), the company behind the Claude chatbot, is set to begin trading on the Nasdaq. It is the first major U.S. AI lab to have a ticker of its own.

The timing could have been better. Tech stocks have had a bruising few weeks, and Jensen Huang’s sudden exit from Nvidia last week shook confidence in the whole AI trade. Even so, demand was strong enough for Anthropic to upsize the deal and price it at $83 a share, above the $70 to $78 range it had marketed. At that price, Anthropic is raising $81.3 billion, which puts it on track to be the biggest IPO on record, ahead of SpaceX’s listing in June.

One of the best-known tech bulls on Wall Street is Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives, who thinks the debut tells investors a lot. “In our view this is a clean read on demand,” the 5-star analyst wrote. In his view, investors were hungry to own a frontier AI developer of this size, and the pricing shows it. He expects OpenAI to follow in 2027.

What stands out most to the analyst is that, for the first time, investors can value a U.S. frontier lab on its own, with no advertising or space business attached. He also points to who is buying in. Nvidia and Google each took $10 billion of a $26 billion private placement at the IPO price, with AMD and other chip and cloud suppliers also on the list. To Ives, the spending the hyperscalers laid out earlier this month and the computing power Anthropic is signing up for are “the same dollars viewed from both ends.”

Anthropic’s filing shows roughly $900 billion in compute commitments stretching over many years. Ives sees that as a long-term demand signal for chipmakers and the clouds that host them. Investors can now read it in a public document instead of piecing it together from capex guidance.

Ives, who ranks among the top 3% of Street stock experts, doesn’t pretend the picture is simple. Third-quarter revenue grew more than twelvefold year over year, but prices are falling and compute bills are landing before the matching revenue is booked. Anthropic made an operating profit in Q2 and slipped to an operating loss in Q3. Ives believes the stock’s direction will depend on which of those quarters turns out to be the real run-rate.

Still, the analyst calls the IPO “a big near-term win for the tech sector,” one that should reassure nervous investors that the AI growth story still has legs. The market is in “a very turbulent, white-knuckle period,” Ives wrote, but that doesn’t change his view that $3 trillion to $4 trillion will go into AI infrastructure over the next few years, with Anthropic a “central player in the buildout.” (To watch Ives’ track record, click here)

This talked-about stock already has 3 positive analyst reviews, making the consensus rating a Strong Buy. (See ANT stock forecast)

data.title: Nvidia vs. Micron – Why Top Analyst Sees More than 110% Upside in One AI Chip Stock
data.description:
Micron (MU) and Nvidia (NVDA) are both benefiting from rising AI demand. RBC Capital analyst Srini Pajjuri has reiterated Outperform ratings on both stocks. His $230 price target for Nvidia implies 52.36% upside. For Micron, his $1,500 target points to 112.68% upside, making Micron his more bullish pick.

After meeting with Micron’s management, Pajjuri remained positive on the stock. He wrote, “We walked away comfortable with our positive stance and view the recent pullback as an excellent opportunity.”  For Nvidia, he pointed to strong chip demand and its product roadmap.

Pajjuri is a five-star analyst on TipRanks, ranked #272 out of 12,578 analysts. He has a 59% success rate and an average return of 30.20% per rating. Here is why he sees more upside in Micron.

Micron’s Tight Memory Supply Could Drive More Upside

Pajjuri expects memory supply to stay tight in 2027 and 2028. After meeting with Micron’s investor relations and treasury teams, he said AI demand and rising HBM use could keep supply below demand. He also sees fewer gains from chip upgrades adding to supply limits.

Micron has already secured much of its future supply. RBC estimates that about three-quarters of its 2027 supply is allocated. It also noted that long-term supply deals cover more than 35% of Micron’s revenue through 2030. Pajjuri noted that these deals give the company better demand visibility. He added, “we see no signs of demand weakening currently.”

Micron has also signed more Supply Commitment Agreements (SCAs). It added 10 new deals in the fourth quarter, taking the total to 26. The agreements cover about 35% of its 2027 DRAM and NAND shipments. They are legally binding and include set pricing bands.

At about 4.2 times estimated 2027 earnings, Pajjuri sees room for Micron’s valuation to rise.

Nvidia’s Strong AI Chip Demand Supports RBC’s Bullish View

Pajjuri also remains bullish on Nvidia after its latest results. The company’s results and outlook came in above market expectations. RBC has raised its FY28 revenue growth outlook to about 75%, from 70% earlier.

Nvidia’s supply commitments have also risen. Pajjuri sees this as a sign of strong demand and confidence in future sales. He believes demand is still well ahead of supply. In his note, he said “demand is significantly outpacing supply.” He also sees Nvidia’s product roadmap as a strength over the next three years.

Nvidia has $227 billion left under its share buyback plan. However, Pajjuri flagged a risk around the company’s leadership. The board has ruled out bringing Jensen Huang back as CEO. He said this “could raise concerns about talent retention.” Even so, RBC sees an attractive risk-reward for Nvidia.

Micron vs. Nvidia: Which Stock Has More Upside?

According to TipRanks data, Micron has a Strong Buy consensus rating, while Nvidia has a Moderate Buy rating. Micron has an average 12-month price target of $1,624.42, implying 130.33% upside. Nvidia has an average price target of $232.59, suggesting 54.08% upside. (See MU Stock Forecast and NVDA Stock Forecast.)

data.title: SpaceX vs. Nvidia: Only One AI Stock Is a ‘Strong Buy’ with 85%+ Upside Ahead of Anthropic’s IPO
data.description:
Anthropic’s IPO puts two major AI stocks in focus: SpaceX (SPCX) and Nvidia (NVDA). The Claude maker priced its shares at $83, valuing the company at about $1.5 trillion ahead of its Nasdaq debut on Thursday, November 19. Both firms have direct ties to Anthropic. Nvidia is investing in the AI company and supplies the chips used to run its models. SpaceX, in turn, provides the computing power Anthropic needs.

The IPO comes at a tough time for both stocks. SpaceX is down 11.96% so far this year, while Nvidia has pulled back sharply from its early October peak following Jensen Huang’s departure, leaving shares down about 16.6% year-to-date. Even so, Wall Street sees room for both stocks to rise. SpaceX has a Strong Buy rating and nearly 89% upside. Nvidia has a Moderate Buy rating and about 50% upside.

SpaceX’s $120.5 Billion Anthropic Deal Could Grow Further

SpaceX has agreed to provide Anthropic with computing power worth up to $120.5 billion through 2029. Anthropic disclosed the deal in its IPO filing. Once all the planned capacity is in place, the AI firm expects to pay about $3.1 billion per month. SpaceX expects to deliver the full capacity by December 2026.

Anthropic is already a major customer for SpaceX. Bloomberg reported that it accounted for 34.5% of SpaceX’s revenue in the third quarter of 2026. It was also the company’s largest single customer.

The deal could also expand. Speaking at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, SPCX CEO Elon Musk said Anthropic was likely to keep renting computing power from SpaceX. He added that the AI firm’s most likely plan was to seek another 10 gigawatts of capacity. Anthropic has not confirmed this figure.

However, the current deal carries some risk. The contracts have initial periods during which they cannot be canceled. Once these periods end in January and March 2027, either side can end the agreements with 90 days’ notice. This means SpaceX may not receive the full $120.5 billion.

Nvidia’s $10B Anthropic Investment and Compute Deal

Nvidia has both an investment and a chip supply link with Anthropic. It has agreed to invest $10 billion in the AI firm through the private placement tied to the IPO. This gives Nvidia a stake in the fast-growing company.

 Nvidia also supplies the GPUs used in Anthropic’s computing deal with SpaceX. As Anthropic expands its AI services, it may need more GPUs from Nvidia. This could support chip sales.

Still, Nvidia sells GPUs to many other AI firms and data center operators. It also faces competition from other chip makers and custom AI chips from cloud providers. This gives Nvidia a wider customer base beyond Anthropic.

SPCX vs. NVDA: Which AI Giant Offers More Upside Now?

Nvidia carries a Moderate Buy consensus. NVDA average 12-month price target of $232.59 implies nearly 50% upside from current levels. By contrast, SpaceX enjoys stronger backing on Wall Street, earning a Strong Buy consensus rating based on 28 Buys, five Holds, and one Sell. SPCX average price target points to about 89% upside over the next year.

data.title: Nebius Stock’s (NBIS) Q3 Sell-Off Looks Like an Opportunity
data.description:
Nebius (NBIS) stock’s Q3 sell-off looks like an attractive opportunity, with shares down almost 64% from their 52-week high. The artificial intelligence (AI) cloud infrastructure provider disappointed investors with another capacity delay, but the underlying business momentum tells a very different story. Rather than pulling back, customers are locking in much larger, multi-year commitments. As CEO Arkady Volozh emphasized on the earnings call, “The demand for AI is real and substantial.”

Q3 2026 revenue surged 571%, and new contract economics improved. I understand the concerns about financing this enormous expansion. Yet customers’ willingness to help fund it makes me more confident. Thus, I rate NBIS stock a Buy.

A Strong Quarter Got Overshadowed

Nebius’ strong Q3 results got overshadowed by another capacity delay. Investors were already questioning Neocloud financing and the sustainability of AI spending. Nebius then shifted some expected revenue into early 2027 because third-party capacity was delayed. Management now expects 2026 revenue near the low end of its $3.0–$3.4 billion range.

Its $7 billion-plus annualized revenue milestone moves from December to February. That is disappointing, although the customer contracts behind the delayed capacity remain intact.

More importantly, the company showed considerable progress. Revenue reached $980.8 million, up 68% sequentially, while AI Cloud revenue grew 643% year-over-year. Group adjusted EBITDA reached $465.8 million, and AI Cloud’s adjusted EBITDA margin was 53.2%. Annualized revenue run rate rose 113% sequentially to $6.4 billion.

Q3 included $325 million of nonrecurring partner revenue. Excluding that contribution, revenue still exceeded four times last year’s total. Customers have also signed over $12 billion of contract value since Q3 began.

The improving contract terms are what impressed me most. Prepayments on Q3 contracts lasting at least a year covered more than 100% of associated capex. That compares with 50%–60% in Q2. Management’s revenue-based payback estimate for comparable contracts improved to 19 months from 22 months. Customers are signing longer agreements at higher prices, helping Nebius recover its spending faster.

I believe this is really important for a company buying expensive graphics processing units (GPUs). Customer funding reduces its dependence on the next debt deal or equity raise.

The Growth Outlook Still Looks Excellent

Meanwhile, the growth outlook still looks excellent heading into 2027. Management expects $12–$13 billion of revenue, roughly four times this year’s level. Four new sites began generating revenue in Q3, with more capacity arriving during Q4. Nebius plans to add over 1 GW annually, increasingly through owned sites. That should give it more control over delivery and operating costs.

Management expects prepayments and investment-grade contract financing to cover 75%–85% of 2027’s $40–$45 billion capex. Microsoft (MSFT) and Meta (META) agreements support that financing strategy. Nebius has over $40 billion of similar committed revenue and ended Q3 with $7.4 billion in cash.

Nvidia’s (NVDA) results on November 17 further strengthened my confidence in that outlook. The chipmaker’s Data Center revenue grew 110%, and Rubin achieved Nvidia’s fastest product ramp. Nebius was among the providers already running Rubin racks. Nvidia also described extraordinary neocloud demand, with $32 billion of commitments extending into 2032 and beyond. Its support depends on financing being secured and capacity becoming operational.

I see those conditions as sensible discipline. They require projects to work before Nvidia’s commitments take effect. So they don’t suggest customers have stopped wanting compute.

Rental pricing offers further evidence. Nebius raised selected on-demand GPU rates roughly 17%–21% from October 1. Across Nvidia’s customer base, some Hopper contracts renewed at up to twice the prior price. B300 rental rates have risen over 60% since introduction. Higher prices on heavily used equipment improve the potential return on each installed dollar.

Nebius is also building services on top of GPU rentals. Token Factory approaches a multi-hundred-million-dollar revenue run rate, with contract value increasing 17-fold sequentially. Managed inference gives existing customers another reason to spend on its platform. Over time, that could make the business more valuable than a basic compute rental operation.

NBIS’ Earnings Could Catch Up Quickly

The market is struggling to value Nebius stock, but I believe earnings could catch up quickly if the company delivers the planned expansion. The stock is now trading at 36x consensus 2028 earnings per share (EPS) of $2.95. That falls to 15.7x 2029 EPS of $6.80. Losses expected through 2027 make today’s P/E less useful. The question is whether new capacity can produce the profits those later estimates imply.

Management targets pre-tax breakeven in Q4 2027. I think that rising rental prices and stronger prepayments make that goal more credible to me. Its full-stack cloud platform also provides ways to earn more from existing customers. If revenue reaches $12-$13 billion next year, earnings could scale rapidly as infrastructure fills. I consider Nebius one of the better-positioned neoclouds for that transition.

Of course, the risks remain substantial. Further construction delays could increase financing needs and dilution. Large customers account for considerable revenue, while GPU replacement costs will consume cash.

Customer advances bring future service obligations, and EBITDA excludes depreciation and financing costs. An eventual supply glut could also reverse today’s pricing gains. This is a speculative investment, but Q3 gave me stronger reasons to accept those risks.

Is NBIS Stock a Buy?

Wall Street rates NBIS a Moderate Buy, based on nine Buys, two Holds, and one Sell. The $260.90 average price target implies about 144% upside. Several analysts lowered their targets after Q3, reflecting the delivery setback.

Conclusion

Nebius still needs to bring capacity online on schedule. Meanwhile, customers are committing more money upfront and accepting higher prices. That is encouraging evidence for both demand and future profitability. I think the sell-off gives investors an attractive opportunity, provided they can tolerate the risks of this enormous buildout.

data.title: Morgan Stanley Says AI Has a Labor Problem — and These 2 ‘Strong Buy’ Stocks Could Cash In
data.description:
Despite recent setbacks, including the scandal surrounding Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang, growing concerns over excessive AI spending, and political uncertainty following the midterm elections, AI remains a key growth driver. However, the opportunities extend beyond chip giants, cloud computing providers, and software developers, with companies responsible for building the infrastructure needed to support AI also positioned to benefit.

Morgan Stanley analyst Stephan Diaz sees considerable potential in the Engineering and Construction (E&C) sector, where demand for skilled workers is outpacing supply. As AI infrastructure projects become larger and more complex, companies with established workforces and specialized expertise could gain a competitive advantage. Diaz believes this labor shortage could translate into stronger growth for leading E&C companies.

“Large Engineering and Construction (E&C) companies have established positions in one of the infrastructure buildout’s key bottlenecks: skilled labor. The training and experience required to develop crews make that capacity difficult to replicate quickly. Most operate in highly specialized verticals such as high and low voltage electric, HVAC, plumbing, and civil. To help safeguard the skilled labor advantage companies in our coverage own, operate, and implement schools, training programs, and staffing companies. Alongside national footprints and strong balance sheets, this supports outsized growth in a narrowly growing non-residential construction market driven by share gains as projects continue to skew larger, more remote, and more complex,” Diaz explained.

With this opportunity in mind, Diaz has highlighted two E&C stocks that could benefit from the growing demand for AI infrastructure. Using the TipRanks database, we’ve taken a closer look at two of his picks, both of which carry Strong Buy consensus ratings from Wall Street. Here’s what makes these companies worth watching.

Comfort Systems USA (FIX)

The first stock we’ll look at, Comfort Systems USA, is a mechanical and electrical contract service provider, based in Houston, Texas. The company is a member of the S&P 500 index and has been since December of last year. Comfort Systems is a holding company with a network of 50-plus operating companies that provide services across 184 locations in the US. The engineering services provided include building and support for mechanical, electrical, modular, and plumbing building systems – the systems necessary to put empty building shells into operation.

Comfort Systems operates through two segments: Mechanical, which covers HVAC, plumbing, process piping, modular and off-site construction, fire protection, and building automation; and Electrical, which includes installation, servicing, and system integration. Its services also span the building lifecycle, including new construction, ongoing maintenance, retrofits, and renovations.

The stock has been volatile this year due to swinging sentiment in the AI sector – it peaked above $2,000 in the summer, and is down 41% in the past six months – but even with that, FIX shares are still up some 18% for the year-to-date.

Looking at the company’s most recent set of financials, we find that Comfort Systems reported $3.77 billion in revenue for 3Q26, up more than 53% year-over-year and more than $365 million better than had been expected. The diluted EPS of $13.91 beat the forecast by $1.06. The company’s outlook is also supported by its growing order backlog, which reached $17.81 billion at the end of Q3, up almost 90% year-over-year.

Morgan Stanley’s Diaz starts with that backlog in his discussion of Comfort Systems and from there he looks at the stock’s prospects in the coming year, writing, “Current backlog levels suggest growth above and beyond our own forecasts when assuming historical conversion rates hold, suggesting opportunity for positive earnings revisions. In addition, strong hyperscaler capex growth, where MS is ahead of street estimates, and a differentiated modular business where FIX has guided to 50% capacity growth in 2027 supports this sentiment. Moreover, the recent de-rating in shares has made for an attractive entry point for a company that recently posted accelerating bookings, guided 2027 to mid-twenties revenue growth, and has the ability to expand its modular offering beyond guided levels due to its net cash position and given current capacity investment plans are with current customers only (mainly 2 hyperscalers).”

Quantifying this stance, Diaz puts an Overweight (i.e., Buy) rating on the stock, along with a $1,410 price target that implies a one-year upside potential of ~24%. (To watch Diaz’s track record, click here)

Wall Street is even more bullish, with the average price target of $1,849 suggesting shares could surge 62% from current levels. All eight recent analyst ratings are Buys, giving FIX stock a unanimous Strong Buy consensus rating. (See FIX stock forecast)

EMCOR Group (EME)

EMCOR, the next stock we’ll look at, is another multi-billion-dollar player in the US construction industry. The company traces its business roots back to 1966, but has been operating in its current incarnation since 1994. EMCOR offers construction services, building services, and industrial services – three core divisions that together make up a vital chunk of the Construction and Engineering segment.

Through its construction services, EMCOR builds and maintains power systems, data centers, and semiconductor plants, and provides them with HVAC installations, fire protection, and modern industrial piping. The building services segment overlaps with HVAC and plumbing, and also includes energy solutions and facility management. Finally, industrial services include work involving refineries, carbon capture, water treatment, and other vital infrastructure. EMCOR works with customers in both the commercial and government sectors.

EMCOR works through a network of about 100 subsidiary operating companies. This network has well over 400 locations across the US, and generated $16.99 billion in revenues last year. And, to build out the array of services it provides, EMCOR has over 47,000 skilled-labor employees, bringing skill and expertise to the ambitious construction projects.

Earlier this month, EMCOR revealed that it has entered an agreement to acquire P1 Construction, a mechanical and electrical contractor serving high-growth markets in the Midwest. The deal was announced as an all-cash transaction, but exact terms were not released.

The last quarterly report covered 3Q26, and showed strong gains from 3Q25. Revenue was up almost 29% year-over-year, and hit $5.54 billion. Earnings were up 46.1%; the non-GAAP EPS of $9.60 beat the forecast by $1.24 per share. And, like Comfort Systems above, EMCOR has a strong work backlog – it reported remaining performance obligations of $18.57 billion at the end of Q3, for a 47.2% year-over-year jump.

All of this explains why analyst Diaz is bullish here. In his coverage for Morgan Stanley, he states, “With a history of solid execution, current backlog levels suggest upside to consensus estimates in 2027, and an undemanding valuation, we view the set-up favorable for EME. Data center work is also a growing share of that backlog, which in the current macro environment will likely be met with question marks. That said, EME’s data center exposure is ~70%/30% cloud vs. AI which should help sentiment. In addition, we find EME’s M&A strategy particularly attractive as the company has shown it can pay below public company multiples for contractors without material data center exposure and then layer its own data center pipeline on top, effectively acquiring skilled craft labor, the industry’s main bottleneck, at a discount to its own multiple. We view EME as a lower beta way to gain exposure to the AI infrastructure demand cycle given its exposure to union labor, more diversified end markets and lower fixed investment risk to data centers vs. FIX.”

Reflecting his confidence, Diaz rates EME as Overweight (i.e., Buy), with a $799 price target suggesting shares could climb ~24% over the next 12 months.

The rest of the Street shares that positive outlook, with 6 Buys and 2 Holds giving EME a Strong Buy consensus rating. At its current price of $644.17, the stock offers a 31.5% potential upside, based on the average analyst target of $849.71. (See EME stock forecast)

data.title: ‘The Peak May Be Here,’ Says Top Investor About Nvidia Stock
data.description:
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) stock briefly looked ready for a comeback after delivering another strong earnings report, but concerns surrounding Jensen Huang’s absence ultimately overshadowed the chip giant’s financial performance. Its encouraging results and outlook initially sent shares soaring nearly 5.5%, suggesting investors were prepared to look beyond the former CEO’s departure. However, that enthusiasm proved short-lived, with the stock reversing course to close Wednesday down 2.9%, extending its losses to about 37% from its early October peak.

At such a steep discount, some investors might be wondering whether Nvidia has finally become too tempting to ignore. However, before pulling the trigger, they may want to hear from investor Victor Dergunov, who ranks among the top 3% of stock experts on TipRanks.

Despite acknowledging the company’s outstanding financial performance, Dergunov believes staying on the sidelines remains the safer choice, warning that its strongest growth years may already be behind it.

The investor focuses on three areas that could determine where NVDA shares go next: revenue growth, profitability, and spending by its largest customers. His conclusion offers little encouragement to those expecting a rebound anytime soon.

“The base case scenario is that 2026 will mark the peak in all three,” Dergunov opined.

That outlook suggests Nvidia could face a prolonged cooling period, potentially limiting future investment returns despite continued operational success.

Consider Nvidia’s latest quarterly performance, which included revenue growth exceeding 100% year-over-year for the second consecutive period. Meanwhile, Nvidia has raised its fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to 75%, up from its previous projection of 70%.

Yet, Dergunov sees reasons for caution, pointing toward the company’s shrinking price-to-sales multiple despite repeated earnings beats. This trend suggests the market has become less willing to reward Nvidia’s achievements with generous valuations.

Profitability presents another concern as the company prepares for higher expenses alongside weaker margins. The company expects GAAP gross margin to range between 71% and 72% next quarter, while operating costs are projected to climb toward $11 billion.

Looking further ahead, Nvidia expects gross margins to recover to between 72% and 73% in fiscal 2028, although that would remain below the 74.8% reported in its latest quarter. Such developments could weigh on earnings potential, regardless of continued strength in customer orders.

Perhaps the biggest concern, however, involves Nvidia’s largest clients and their appetite for expensive computing infrastructure. Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, and Oracle have poured billions into expanding data centers, helping drive the semiconductor manufacturer’s extraordinary sales figures. Dergunov calculates that their combined capital expenditures have now exceeded operating cash flow, raising doubts about how long this pace can continue. Should these tech companies begin moderating investments, Nvidia could face a tougher environment than its latest quarterly figures suggest.

Ultimately, Dergunov believes investors should distinguish between owning a successful enterprise and purchasing an attractive investment at current prices.

“Strong quarterly results do not mean above-market shareholder returns,” the investor wrote.

For now, Dergunov assigns NVDA shares a Hold (i.e., Neutral) rating, suggesting investors may be better served waiting for greater clarity before committing additional capital. (To watch Dergunov’s track record, click here)

Wall Street, however, remains more bullish on Nvidia’s prospects, with the stock earning a Moderate Buy consensus rating based on 30 Buys, 13 Holds, and just one Sell. Still, analysts were far more enthusiastic just two weeks ago, before a wave of downgrades brought the number of Hold recommendations to 13. Nonetheless, the average 12-month price target of $232.59 suggests an upside potential of 54% from current levels. (See NVDA stock forecast)

data.title: 3 ‘Strong Buy’ High-Risk Stocks That Could Deliver 100% or More Gains
data.description:
Aurora Innovation (AUR), SanDisk Corp. (SNDK), and Praxis Precision Medicines (PRAX) are three high-risk, high-reward stocks analysts see as having massive upside potential. Wall Street rates each a Strong Buy and projects at least 100% upside. AUR leads the pack with about 193% upside potential.

These companies operate in fast-changing markets. In such markets, investor sentiment can shift quickly as conditions change. That volatility creates significant risk, but also the potential for huge gains. This is especially true if the companies deliver on their growth strategies.

These stocks have a beta greater than two. In other words, their shares are more than twice as volatile as the broader market.

Aurora Innovation (AUR)

Aurora is a U.S. self-driving tech startup known for the Aurora Driver. This advanced platform combines hardware, software, and data services to enable self-driving. Aurora was founded in 2017 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. It is now racing toward the commercial rollout of its technology.

On Wall Street, AUR has a Strong Buy consensus, with six Buys and two Holds issued over the past three months. The average AUR price target of $11.43 suggests about 193% upside ahead.

SanDisk Corp. (SNDK)

This is an American storage company. It develops and makes storage products based on NAND flash memory. This refers to non-volatile memory, meaning it stores data even when power is off. This technology is used in products such as solid-state drives, memory cards, and USB drives.

On Wall Street, SNDK carries a Strong Buy consensus, with 11 Buys and three Holds assigned over the past three months. This comes with an average price target of $2,131, suggesting about 175% upside.

Praxis Precision Medicines (PRAX)

data.title: VIDEO: Mining Without Digging: Modern Mining CEO Jeet Basi on Recovering Critical Metals From E-Waste
data.description:
On the day Modern Mining Technology Corp. (MDRN) begins trading on the New York Stock Exchange, CEO Jeet Basi joins Chris Versace to explain how the company recovers gold, silver, palladium, and copper from discarded electronics without burning anything.

He walks through the process, explains why a ton of circuit boards can hold roughly 130 times the gold of a ton of typical ore, and lays out the plan to put its IPO proceeds toward a first commercial plant in North Carolina, with revenue targeted for late 2027 to early 2028.

If you’re looking for more information on Modern Mining, please see the company’s webpage.

Transcript

Chris Versace: Hey everyone, Chris Versace here. From time to time, we get a lot of questions about gold and critical materials here at the Pro Portfolio. That’s not surprising. Gold prices were around $4,300 an ounce when we entered 2026 and ran up near $5,400 in February. They’ve bounced around quite a bit since then, but since August they’ve traded off and are hovering around $3,900 an ounce as I talk with you today.

As part of that conversation about gold, critical materials and critical minerals, we’ve got a really good discussion today with the CEO of Modern Mining, Jeet Basi. Jeet, welcome, and thank you so much. My understanding is it’s a really busy day for you, as you begin trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol MDRN.

Jeet Basi: That’s right, Chris. First and foremost, it’s a pleasure to be here, my friend. I appreciate the opportunity to talk about our company on such a tremendous platform, and I’m looking forward to connecting with you, your team and the broader audience behind you. Today’s an exciting day. It’s been a tremendous journey, all leading up to this milestone. Today we completed our IPO, and we are a publicly listed company on the New York Stock Exchange.

Chris Versace: If I remember correctly from doing my homework, you’re a pre-revenue company. You’ve had a development facility in North Carolina where you’ve been showing people what you can do with your proprietary process. The key here is that there’s a growing mountain of e-waste every year, and I’ll ask you more about that in a second. What you’re looking to do is run a smart, focused recycling process that gets these critical materials out and then repurposes them for other uses, correct?

Jeet Basi: That’s spot on. Our goal at Modern Mining is to produce as much metal as we physically can without digging a single hole, the way the traditional mining industry does. Our focus is electronic waste. We don’t search for gold. We already know where the gold, silver, copper and palladium are. They’re in the devices we throw away every day.

Chris Versace: Right, and that’s everything from smartphones, tablets and PCs to, I imagine, digital cameras, screens or monitors, TVs, that sort of thing.

Jeet Basi: You bet. All of the above and more. Any device that has an electrical plug, a power source or any kind of circuitry contains ample precious, commodity and critical metals, and that’s of interest to us.

Step one, we bring that equipment into our facility. This is all end-of-life material that would otherwise end up in a landfill. Step two, inside the facility, we very specifically extract and recover the key valuable metals. Step three, we bring those metals back into the commodity markets so they can be repurposed into new devices and new goods for everyone to use.

Chris Versace: Okay, a couple of questions. When we talk about key materials, I mentioned gold a little while ago, but are silver, palladium and copper some of the others you’re looking at?

Jeet Basi: Yes, those are the four we’re focusing on at the outset. As you can imagine, within this vast mountain of electronic waste and scrap, a number of other metals exist as well, and we may look to bring them into our workflow in the future. But you’re right, Chris. Right now, our focus is primarily gold, silver, palladium and copper.

Chris Versace: Walk us through the process. When I get rid of my devices, I might recycle them at Best Buy, through Apple or with some other group. You said you bring the e-waste in. Where is it coming from?

Jeet Basi: Exactly the way you mentioned. Many original equipment manufacturers have take-back programs, and they’re always looking for homes for those products, so we can offer them an outlet. There are also primary recyclers, the 1-800-GOT-JUNK? type of companies. These are our colleagues. They work around the clock collecting all kinds of things, and when they find a pocket of electronic scrap and don’t know what to do with it, they call people like us.

So, it’s a wide variety. It could be someone in your family looking to get rid of e-waste, or it could be a major original equipment manufacturer with a big buyback program. There are also government recycling facilities. The whole ecosystem is quite diverse.

Chris Versace: Interesting. Going back to e-waste, as I look at my notes, we talked about the obvious candidates like smartphones and laptops. But I was a little surprised to see refrigerators, washing machines, microwaves, toasters and even vacuum cleaners. It’s all fair game?

Jeet Basi: It’s all fair game, because each of those devices, as you mentioned, has a power source, a power cord and a circuit, and all those components carry value. Our big focus is extracting value from those key components. The overall list of e-waste categories is large and diverse. Some UN publications identify 52 different categories, with several items within each. So, hundreds of devices fit the term e-waste, and we’re just getting started.

Chris Versace: There are a lot of forecasts for e-waste tonnage, and they show the typical up-and-to-the-right curve. But I think there’s another way to look at this. When you see capital being pushed into an area to solve a problem, it tells you that either the problem needs to be addressed or there’s an opportunity there. Getting ready to talk with you, I saw that Mitsubishi and Sumitomo are moving into e-waste processing, and I think Cyclic Materials is as well. From your perspective, it’s a validation point. Where are you compared to these companies, or is everyone in the early days?

Jeet Basi: I think most of us are in the early days. The industry itself is in its infancy, and the upside is so big that there’s room for many players. We welcome more people to the space, because if we want to get serious about recovering metal from all this waste, there’s a lot of room to play. With rising metal prices and long mine development timelines, where putting a mine into production takes 10 to 15 years, recovering metals from discarded electronics is an increasingly important topic. That’s exactly the gap Modern Mining and some of these other companies are aiming to help fill. The more the merrier, as we say.

Chris Versace: Talk to me about your process. I understand you’re trying to minimize waste as you work through the waste, so there’s no incineration, and I believe you have a proprietary process. Tell us about it as best you can.

Jeet Basi: You bet. The key differentiator is that, unlike the status quo in the industry, we don’t burn anything. Our recovery is based on what you could call washing. We focus primarily on waste printed circuit boards, which are our startup feedstock. That material comes into our plant, and we use techniques very similar to conventional mining: crushing, screening and milling. As you can imagine, e-waste comes into our facility in many different shapes and forms.

Chris Versace: Of course. Something out of a refrigerator is very different from something out of a laptop.

Jeet Basi: Exactly. To process it efficiently, we have to homogenize it. We run the material through a cutter or shredder. A circuit board that might be 24 inches by six inches gets chopped into one-inch fragments. We then mill, pulverize and grind those fragments down to a powder that looks like a bucket of flour.

Inside that powder are discrete grains of plastic, fiberglass, epoxies and resins, but also discrete grains of valuable metals like gold, silver, copper, aluminum and others. Once we’ve achieved that sand-like consistency, we apply gravitational force to the mixture and exploit the difference in density between metals and plastics. All the valuable metals separate into one stream, which we call metallic sands concentrate, and the plastics and other barren materials separate into a second, non-metallic stream. In doing so, we pre-concentrate the metals.

That’s the middle step. The last step is where the real fun happens. We use selective chemistry to isolate the individual metals in that metallic mixture, separate and enrich them, and produce enriched metal products on the back end.

Chris Versace: You’re focused on those key metals. I’m curious, what happens to the plastics and other non-metals?

Jeet Basi: That’s a great question, and different companies do different things. We have partnerships with companies that use those plastics as a feedstock for their own downstream processes, mainly because of the energy content in the plastic. So, what you could call waste for us is actually an input for someone else.

Chris Versace: Is that a revenue stream for you, even if a smaller one?

Jeet Basi: Right now, it’s a net-neutral stream. As we grow, we’ll try to make it revenue positive.

Chris Versace: Two more questions on the process. First, is it automated or people intensive? Second, what about hazardous materials like lead and mercury?

Jeet Basi: In our demonstration facility, I must admit we’ve been very lean and disciplined with our capital. We don’t have the bells and whistles. It’s very manual, very step by step. The design we envision for a commercial plant will be fully automated, with automated feedback loops, instrumentation and control systems. The workforce required to operate one of our facilities will be many times smaller than at a traditional mine, and I’m quite proud of that. The reason we can do that is that our feedstock is, in many cases, more than 100 times richer than a traditional mine.

Chris Versace: Why do you say that? That sounds surprising.

Jeet Basi: Think about it this way. Mother Nature is very unpredictable, whereas electronics are very prescriptive, man-made products. Manufacturers know exactly how much copper they need for that machine to do its job.

Compare that to an average gold mine. One ton of ore contains roughly one gram of gold, so you have to process that ton of rock to extract about one gram. If we take the same weight of our feedstock, specifically the printed circuit boards in electronic scrap, one ton contains roughly 130 grams of gold on average, at least in our feedstock. And that’s just the gold, not including the copper, silver and palladium. It’s because it’s an engineered product.

Chris Versace: So, it’s a manufactured product, but from your perspective, it’s a target-rich environment. That helps explain some things I was reading. I believe the IEA has said that the success of what you and others are doing could reduce the number of mines needed in the coming years by something like 25% to 40%.

Jeet Basi: I haven’t seen that stat, but it wouldn’t be surprising if the numbers lined up that way.

Chris Versace: Let’s talk about the IPO. You mentioned your target facility, and my understanding is that, with the proceeds in hand, that’s the focal point for the next year. You’re hoping to be revenue generating by 2028, or maybe a little sooner?

Jeet Basi: That’s exactly what we’re targeting: the back end of 2027 into the early part of 2028 for commercial production and commercial revenue.

Chris Versace: If we look at what you’ve raised, I believe it’s $40 million, less fees, which we’ll see in the final numbers. How far does that carry you on the build-out? Does it take you all the way with some cushion, or will you need to hit certain hurdles and possibly raise more capital?

Jeet Basi: It’s the former. It allows us to fully build out our first facility, which we’re aiming to stand up in North Carolina, and it gives us an 18- to 24-month runway in total. So, if we’re starting revenue at the back end of 2027 or early 2028, we’re fully funded into the middle to back half of 2028.

Chris Versace: I’d imagine you wouldn’t go public if you weren’t confident and comfortable. But for folks who may not know the ins and outs of the business, coming out of the development stage, have any companies said they’d be interested in your materials as you ramp up? Or have you gone further and announced contracts? Any color that might give listeners more comfort that there’s a master plan at work?

Jeet Basi: For sure. One of the things that gets our team most excited is that this isn’t a lab story. We’ve made actual product in our demonstration plant, sent it to third parties for analysis and, on the back of that analysis, made actual sales. So, we already have buyers for product from the demonstration facility.

We have not yet locked in a long-term offtake partner. We don’t necessarily want to put all our eggs in one basket at this point. We want to give our stakeholders maximum exposure to the commodity run. Once we reach critical mass, we may look at longer-term offtakes, but right now we’ve been selling into the spot market. It’s a very liquid market, and it’s been quite fruitful for our efforts.

Chris Versace: Excellent. When do you plan to break ground, and will you be open to visitors?

Jeet Basi: Absolutely, Chris. We hope to break ground in early 2027, and we’d love to host you and your audience, whether at the commercial plant or the demo plant. You’re always welcome. I also want to thank you and your audience. You’ve been some of our strongest supporters to date, and we really appreciate the patience you’ve shown us. These are exciting times, and we’re happy to host you anytime.

Chris Versace: That would be wonderful, but you’re not getting out of here that soon. I have one or two more questions. You said earlier that those are the four metals you’re focused on initially, which suggests there might be others. Do you need to add new capabilities to go beyond the big four?

Jeet Basi: We haven’t publicly disclosed the other metals in our feedstock, but published literature describes some of the other elements in electronic scrap. For example, you see lithium and black mass in some types of scrap, and scrap from permanent magnets contains more rare earths, along with cobalt, nickel and manganese. These are all critical metals found in electronic waste.

While we aren’t focusing on them today, we may in the future, following the necessary R&D and process development. We’ll look to grow the business into those verticals as the opportunities arise. But those things won’t happen in the first commercial plant. We’ll need to add modules and processes to bring those metals to market.

Chris Versace: I won’t say it’s a no-brainer, but as someone peering in, if you’re taking in this waste, you want to maximize what you can pull out of it. The top four might be the largest opportunity, but there’s still something left on the table to monetize.

Jeet Basi: One of our biggest passions is making sure we extract every piece of value we can, and as we grow, we’ll certainly look to do exactly that.

Chris Versace: All right, Jeet, before we wrap up, and again, I know you’re very busy today, is there anything about Modern Mining we didn’t touch on that we should?

Jeet Basi: Chris, you know the space as well as anyone, and the questions kept me on my toes. The one other thing I’d share that’s unique to our business relative to traditional mining is this. I love mining. I spent 20 years in the industry. I love the people, the science, the travel and the role traditional mining plays in supporting society and providing the raw ingredients that move it forward. But one element always frustrated me, and that’s that it’s finite.

Every mine in production today, and every mine in exploration that will eventually be in production, depletes its resource a little bit year after year until it eventually goes to zero. The feedstock we process, electronic scrap, has no expiration and no geology, and its quantity is growing every year.

Chris Versace: As you were describing that, I was thinking that whether you’re drilling for oil or mining gold or some other material, you have to dig so many holes and hope it pays, as they say, even with better technology. But when I replace a screen, a monitor or a refrigerator, I’m most likely replacing it with another one. That says this e-waste cycle could get bigger, and it’s not going away over time.

Jeet Basi: We view our feedstock as growing with every upgrade cycle that comes to market, whether that’s a new set of monitors, the newest phone or the newest AI data centers. At some point, that equipment reaches the end of its useful life and adds to an already large mountain of electronic scrap. That happens every year, so we see our feedstock growing rather than depleting like our traditional mining peers.

Chris Versace: I have to apologize, because I said we were almost done, and now you’ve sparked another question. Compare the iPhone 18 to, say, the iPhone 6. We have a lot more processing power, a lot more memory and a lot more on the printed circuit board. Does that make newer, more advanced devices more target rich for Modern Mining?

Jeet Basi: It depends on the sector and industry, but broadly speaking, newer devices arguably have less gold and a lot more of some of the other metals outside the big four. People are getting smarter. Gold is expensive, so manufacturers try to use less of it. The gold content in devices is falling, but the content of other critical metals is rising, and so are their commodity prices. Gold is also a lot more expensive now. We see that as a net positive for companies like ours that are trying to recover these metals and bring them back into the supply chain.

Chris Versace: Jeet Basi, congratulations again on the IPO, and thank you for joining us. I think we’ll come back to you in six to nine months as you’re building your facility, to see where things stand, and I hope you’ll join us. One last thing: for folks who want to learn more about Modern Mining, where should they go? We’ll link your latest investor presentation in the notes, but is there anywhere else they can go to learn more about e-waste?

Jeet Basi: The key spot is our website, modernmining.com, which has links to the various parts of our business. We have a very strong investor relations team, so give them a call. They’re happy to answer any question in whatever detail you’d like. We always like to connect with our stakeholders, and you’re always welcome. I appreciate the opportunity, Chris.

Chris Versace: Awesome. Thank you so much, Jeet.

data.title: Billionaire Investor Stanley Druckenmiller Got Out of AI Chip Stocks in Time. Is It Time to Get Back In?
data.description:
Stanley Druckenmiller built his reputation on knowing when to get in and when to get out. He helped George Soros bet against the British pound in 1992, ran money for three decades without a losing year, and was one of the first big investors to buy Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) for the AI boom. He has also said he regrets selling that stake in 2024. His latest filing shows he spent the summer getting out of chip stocks, and judging by the selloff that followed, his timing looks good again.

Semiconductor shares sold off hard after the quarter ended, and Nvidia fell further when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO last week. Then came Nvidia’s third-quarter report last night. Revenue of $115.8 billion beat the roughly $109 billion Wall Street expected, and guidance of about $130 billion for the current quarter came in above forecasts. That has done little to improve sentiment, however, with the stock unable to hold its premarket gains and tilting into the red at today’s open.

Druckenmiller’s Duquesne Family Office filed its 13F on Monday, showing holdings as of Sept. 30. The portfolio shrank to $4.47 billion across 65 positions, from $5.21 billion across 95 at the end of June.

The biggest move came in Taiwan Semiconductor (NYSE:TSM). The investor cut that stake by 94%, from about 589,700 shares to 32,700. He also sold all of his AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) and Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) shares, positions worth around $42 million and $79 million at the end of June, and exited Arm Holdings (NASDAQ:ARM) and Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX) as well. Outside of chips, he sold his entire Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) position of 336,300 Class A shares, a stake he had bought in the second quarter.

That doesn’t mean he gave up on tech hardware altogether. Duquesne nearly tripled its Seagate (NASDAQ:STX) stake to 341,790 shares, worth about $315 million, and opened a roughly $37 million position in Western Digital (NASDAQ:WDC). Both companies make the hard drives that fill data centers.

Much of the new money went elsewhere. Druckenmiller opened three gold miner positions of about $42 million to $44 million each in Newmont (NYSE:NEM), Barrick Mining (NYSE:B) and Agnico Eagle (NYSE:AEM). He also bought into SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) with 202,125 shares worth about $30.5 million, and took an 80,100-share position in Palantir (NASDAQ:PLTR) worth about $15 million. Genetic testing company Natera (NASDAQ:NTRA) remains his largest holding by a wide margin, with 3.16 million shares worth about $1.31 billion, or 29% of the portfolio.

A 13F only shows where things stood on Sept. 30, and Druckenmiller has made clear that the picture has moved on since. Speaking at the TomorrowX conference on Tuesday, he said his firm is “basically staying away” from stocks and that he owns almost nothing he held in January. He added that he can hardly remember a time when he had less clarity on where markets will be a year from now, citing a tighter Fed and inflation running above target. Nvidia’s strong outlook may pull other investors back into chips, but the billionaire known for his timing is sitting this one out for now.

data.title: ‘Not So Fast,’ Says Top Investor About Nvidia Stock
data.description:
For the first time in its 33-year history, Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) held an earnings call without Jensen Huang. The chipmaker released its third-quarter fiscal 2027 report on Tuesday. Board chair Harvey Jones opened the call by addressing the question that had been hanging over the stock. Hours earlier, Huang had posted a statement on X saying he would be “honored” to return as CEO if the board asked. Jones said the board does not intend to bring him back.

With that out of the way, investors can’t seem to decide what to make of the quarter. Results and guidance both beat forecasts, and the shares climbed before the bell on Wednesday. Once trading opened, though, the early rally faded, and the stock has been flipping between small gains and losses.

An investor using the pseudonym The Techie (TT), who ranks among the top 4% of investors on TipRanks, gives Nvidia credit for the quarter but separates the company from its shares. In TT’s view, the business keeps getting stronger, but nothing around the stock has improved.

Revenue reached $115.8 billion, up 103% year over year. That was well ahead of Nvidia’s own $108 billion guide and the roughly $109 billion Wall Street expected. Adjusted EPS of $2.68 beat the consensus estimate of about $2.47. For the current quarter, Nvidia guided to $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, against forecasts near $125 billion. It also raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to about 75% from 70%. Not everything was positive. Gross margin is guided down to 71%–72% from 74.9% in the third quarter, the outlook assumes no data center compute sales to China, and Nvidia has stopped shipping licensed Hopper chips there.

TT’s main concern is where the growth is coming from. Sales to AI clouds, industrial and enterprise customers nearly tripled YoY to $47.5 billion. TT notes that this group includes the neoclouds, the smaller cloud providers that depend most on Nvidia’s financial backing to fund their build-outs. Interim CEO Colette Kress said the fiscal 2028 outlook takes customers’ access to capital into account. What bothers TT is that the person behind many of these deals has left while the commitments keep growing. TT points to Elon Musk, who wrote on X on Nov. 14 that many of Nvidia’s supply deals were “a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract.”

The CEO search adds to the unease. The board will consider internal and external candidates, but it hasn’t named anyone yet. TT doesn’t think the market has fully accounted for losing a founder who was so central to the company and its suppliers. Regulators are another weight. On Tuesday morning, the board set up a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee.

On valuation, Nvidia trades at roughly 17x trailing earnings, which looks inexpensive. TT’s answer is that the stock has been cheap for some time, and with good reason. TT sees the post-earnings jump as a bounce that was due after a steep slide, not a reward for a beat everyone expected.

“I do not find the stock attractive enough at current levels, given how much remains unresolved around its leadership, its regulatory exposure, and its financing commitments,” the 5-star investor summed up. “I would not chase the bounce, and I expect headlines to keep driving the stock until the board names a permanent CEO.”

All told, the stock stays a Hold for The Techie. (To watch The Techie’s track record, click here)

On the Street, 13 analysts are also on the sidelines, while an additional 30 Buys and 1 Sell all add up to a Moderate Buy consensus view. At $229.33, the average price target implies shares will gain 48% over the coming months. (See NVDA stock forecast)

data.title: Why Take-Two Interactive Stock Is Surging Today and Why This Investor Thinks It’s Time to Run for the Hills
data.description:
Take-Two Interactive (NASDAQ:TTWO) shares are climbing about 5.5% on Wednesday, as excitement surrounding the long-awaited release of Grand Theft Auto VI gives investors another reason to buy. The highly anticipated title is finally arriving on Thursday, November 19, after repeated delays, with record-breaking preorders pointing toward a potentially historic debut for Rockstar Games.

The enthusiasm comes at an important moment for TTWO, which has experienced significant volatility ahead of the launch. With expectations running high, Wall Street is betting that GTA VI will deliver blockbuster sales while generating additional revenue through online purchases for years to come.

Yet, investor Boris Marjanovic believes the market may be overlooking a serious long-term threat. He has assigned Take-Two a Sell rating, arguing that AI could eventually undermine the very financial model supporting its lofty valuation.

Marjanovic’s concerns extend well beyond whether the upcoming release will live up to its considerable hype. His bearish outlook focuses on how technological developments could change the way consumers create, access, and spend money on video games.

“I believe AI makes that a bad long-term bet,” Marjanovic wrote.

The investor points to tools from Google and Roblox that already allow users to develop playable experiences through simple instructions. Meanwhile, other software can reconstruct older titles with limited input, suggesting traditional publishers could face growing competition from amateur creators.

Such capabilities could eventually give gaming enthusiasts alternatives that require little financial commitment, potentially weakening demand for expensive commercial releases. Marjanovic also anticipates unauthorized adaptations of GTA VI appearing relatively soon after launch, although he considers another financial risk far more concerning.

Marjanovic believes the greater risk lies in the revenue Take-Two generates long after customers purchase their initial copies. During the previous fiscal year, virtual currency, downloadable content, advertising, and related transactions generated $5.20 billion, accounting for 78% of total sales. That dependence leaves the publisher vulnerable if players gradually shift their spending toward competing entertainment options. A mere 5% reduction in revenue from recurrent consumer spending would translate into an annual loss of approximately $260 million.

Still, Marjanovic acknowledges that Rockstar possesses advantages that could help protect its position over time. The enduring popularity of GTA V demonstrates how successful franchises can maintain loyal audiences, while AI-assisted development might also reduce future production expenses. However, those possibilities haven’t convinced him that the current stock price offers an appealing investment opportunity.

His discounted cash flow model assumes technological competition will eventually reduce annual sales by $500 million, partially offset by lower development expenses. Under these assumptions, the resulting impact on cash generation reaches $200 million annually by fiscal 2031.

“I value Take-Two at $163 a share… If AI has no net effect, my estimate rises to $176 a share,” Marjanovic noted.

Ultimately, Marjanovic isn’t predicting that GTA VI will disappoint when it reaches consumers this week. He simply believes today’s enthusiasm overlooks the possibility that tomorrow’s gaming landscape could make Take-Two’s future profits much harder to sustain.

data.title: ‘Not Out of the Woods,’ Says Top Investor About Rocket Lab Stock
data.description:
Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) has had a mixed few weeks, and the stock has only listened to the bad half. Its third-quarter earnings report on Nov. 9 showed record sales and a wave of new contracts, and on Nov. 14 its small Electron rocket flew for the 100th time. But Neutron, the bigger rocket the company is counting on, won’t fly until 2027 after a delay announced in October, and losses are getting deeper. A short rally after the report faded within days, and the shares have since handed most of the gains back to the market. The stock now sits ~64% below its late-May peak.

Considering the company’s excellent growth profile, could investors have an opportunity to load up at a discount? A top investor using the moniker of The Asian Investor (TAI) went through the report to see whether that’s the case.

The investor gives Rocket Lab credit for the top line. Revenue jumped 73% year over year to a record $267.8 million, beating Wall Street’s forecast and the top of management’s own range. Backlog grew 52% from the prior quarter to about $3.6 billion. That’s split fairly evenly between launch services and Space Systems, the unit that builds satellites and spacecraft hardware. Management expects fourth-quarter revenue of $270 million to $290 million, which would take full-year sales close to $1 billion, roughly 63% above 2025.

The bottom line is another matter. Rocket Lab lost $79.7 million in the quarter, more than four times its loss a year earlier and wider than analysts expected. TAI, who ranks among the top 3% of investors on TipRanks, blames heavier R&D and operating spending as the company builds Neutron, its medium-lift rocket, plus a $27.3 million loss on extinguishment of debt. Another $21.3 million went to transaction costs, mostly for the pending $8 billion purchase of satellite operator Iridium Communications.

The slide also hasn’t made the stock cheap. With a market cap of about $36 billion, Rocket Lab trades at roughly 40x trailing 12-month sales. Three other companies that rely heavily on government contracts are far cheaper. L3Harris trades at under 3x sales, Redwire at around 3x, and Intuitive Machines at around 3.5x. TAI thinks the market is pricing in a lot of growth, and much of it depends on a rocket that hasn’t flown yet.

Which brings us to Neutron, the deciding factor. On Oct. 14, Rocket Lab pushed the rocket’s debut into 2027 after finding flaws in a fuel tank component, and it hasn’t set a new date. TAI expects the first flight in the first half of next year. A clean launch would lift the mood around the stock and open up a new business carrying heavier payloads. Another slip would put even more attention on the losses.

“With management not providing enough clarity about when it will launch its medium-to-heavy-duty Neutron rocket and heavy losses weighing on Rocket Lab’s financial performance, I expect a weak investment setup at least for the next several months,” the 5-star investor summed up.

Accordingly, TAI rates Rocket Lab stock a Sell. (To watch The Asian Investor’s track record, click here)

data.title: ‘No Respect,’ Says Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) spent the first half of the year as one of the hottest names in the AI trade, but the tables have turned since then. Doubts over how long the memory boom can run, a chip selloff after the midterm elections and the leadership turmoil at Nvidia have all weighed on the memory giant.

Today, investors hoped Nvidia’s strong third-quarter results would spark a rebound, but that hasn’t happened, and the stock is down once again. The shares now sit about 43% below their record close in late June.

Yet, for those wondering if the stock will reclaim its June highs any time soon, investor Keithen Drury, who contributes to The Motley Fool, thinks the market has badly misjudged how long this upswing will last.

The investor accepts that memory has always moved in cycles of shortage and oversupply, and that the good times usually fade within a year or so. Drury argues this cycle has broken that pattern. AI data centers are taking every chip the industry can make, and Micron and its rivals have committed their output far into the future. Management backed that up at Micron’s fiscal fourth-quarter report on Sept. 30, saying it expects supply to be even tighter in 2027 and 2028 than it was in 2026, a year when memory was already scarce. More than 75% of Micron’s 2027 output is already spoken for.

In Drury’s view, that outlook should have reset the way investors value the stock. So far, the share price shows no sign of it. Micron trades at less than 5 times forward earnings, compared with about 18 times for the S&P 500, according to FactSet. The investor agrees that a cyclical company deserves to trade at a discount to the broader market, but considers this gap much too big. Even a multiple of about 10 times earnings, well below where Micron traded earlier this year, would be enough for the stock to more than double within a year or so, by Drury’s reckoning.

Looking further out, the investor is even more upbeat. Drury expects AI infrastructure spending to continue until at least 2030, which would keep Micron producing at full tilt and earning close to peak profits for years. The company also has several new plants due to open over the next few years. The investor expects customers to snap up that extra capacity as soon as it comes online, so it should add to growth rather than create a glut.

As for claiming June’s highs again, Drury thinks that hurdle will be overcome, and then  some. “I could see Micron’s stock tripling over the next three years as its valuation rises to a more respectable level and the market realizes that this cycle will last much longer,” Drury summed up. Pajjuri also sees Micron benefiting from longer-term customer agreements, which offer greater predictability regarding future orders. Meanwhile, the company’s plans to distribute surplus funds through repurchases could provide additional support for its valuation.

data.title: ‘Ready for More Pain?’ Investor Asks About Strategy Stock
data.description:
These are rough days once again for Strategy (NASDAQ:MSTR) shareholders. Bitcoin is hovering near a three-month low and has fallen below the price Strategy paid for its coins on average. Index provider MSCI is about to show the stock the door, and the common shares now trade below the company’s own preferred stock.

Strategy’s fall rally has all but evaporated, and the stockslipped under $100 on Tuesday. It was the first time the common had traded beneath its STRC preferred since mid-August. MSCI said on Nov. 11 that it will drop Strategy from its USA Index after the Nov. 30 close, which also takes it out of the World and ACWI benchmarks.

So, with the stock falling again today, and now down by 55% over the past year, should investors mull over getting some exposure here? Only if you’re ready for more pain, says an investor using the moniker Capital Minded (CM).

CM is a long-term bitcoin bull and thinks the index exit is the smaller worry. CM is more bothered by where Strategy’s money has been going. In the third quarter, the company raised $5.41 billion from common stock sales, but only $588.1 million of it, about 11%, bought bitcoin. Most of the rest was held as cash or spent supporting STRC, a preferred stock that pays a 12% annual dividend, after its price fell below the $100 par value. Strategy also sold 5,552 bitcoins during the quarter to help pay preferred dividends. The most recent weekly filing looks the same: of $244.7 million raised, $33.4 million went to bitcoin and $206.3 million went to STRC buybacks.

To CM, this means common shareholders are now paying for the preferred holders. Strategy’s BTC Yield, its own measure of bitcoin per share, stood at negative 3.7% for the year as of late October. Each share now carries less bitcoin than it did when the year began.

The bills keep growing. Preferred dividends reached $419.6 million in Q3, roughly three times the year-ago amount. The software business produced only $89.6 million of gross profit, on revenue that fell 3% year over year. CM gives Strategy credit for building a $4.75 billion dollar reserve. But that cash is set aside for dividends and interest. Between September 2027 and September 2028, holders could also hand back about $5.9 billion of convertible notes for cash. The first $1.01 billion of those notes converts at roughly $183 a share, far above today’s price. CM argues that covering both would cost common shareholders one way or another.

The investor does praise management for getting STRC back to its $100 par value on Nov. 4, after 165 days below it. That matters because Strategy only sells new STRC at $100 or above, and those sales raise money without creating more common shares. STRC has since dipped just under $100, though, so that door is closed again for now.

Index funds hold about 13 million MSTR shares, and CM sees their selling as a short-term hit. The bigger problem is that the stock only beats holding bitcoin when buyers pay a premium for it. Strategy has been the fourth-largest U.S. issuer of capital this year, and losing MSCI’s automatic buyers makes that premium harder to win back.

CM would rethink the call if bitcoin purchases start to outpace STRC buybacks, preferred sales restart at par, and bitcoin per share grows for two quarters in a row. Until then, Capital Minded would rather own bitcoin directly and rates Strategy stock a Sell. (To watch Capital Minded’s track record, click here)

data.title: SK Hynix vs. Micron: One AI Stock Is Good, the Other Is Better, Says Top Investor
data.description:
Nvidia’s earnings reports are usually read as a verdict on the whole AI trade. Tuesday’s report also worked as a progress check on the companies that sell it memory. Alongside a third-quarter beat, Nvidia said its commitments to buy parts from suppliers jumped during the quarter, mostly because of multiyear deals to lock in memory. Few companies stand to gain more from that than SK Hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY) and Micron (NASDAQ:MU), two of the three makers of the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) that sits inside Nvidia’s AI chips.

Nvidia put those commitments at $390 billion, up from $279 billion three months earlier. Both memory stocks jumped before the bell on Wednesday and have swung back and forth since the open, a sign of how nervous the market still is about the AI trade. Either way, both have a lot of ground to make up. Micron is still about 41% below its June high, and SK Hynix’s U.S.-listed shares are roughly 38% under their September peak.

Top investor Leo Sun, who contributes to The Motley Fool and ranks among the top 3% of investors on TipRanks, has been weighing which of the two is the better long-term AI holding.

The investor starts with what they share. DRAM, not NAND, brings in the bulk of sales at both companies, and both are counting on HBM, a high-density type of DRAM that feeds Nvidia’s data center GPUs, to power their near-term growth. SK Hynix, based in South Korea, trails only Samsung in DRAM, with Idaho-based Micron in third place.

Where they split, in Sun’s view, is timing. SK Hynix was the first to mass-produce HBM3 in 2022, and that head start made it Nvidia’s main supplier just as AI spending took off. It moved on to HBM3E in 2024 and HBM4 this year. Micron passed on HBM3 entirely, entered with HBM3E in 2024, and has also reached HBM4. Demand for its chips still runs ahead of what it can make. There is a knock-on effect, too. Every bit of factory space the two put toward HBM is space they can’t use for ordinary DRAM and NAND, which has left the rest of the memory market short of supply.

The growth on both sides is huge. SK Hynix grew revenue 47% year over year in 2025 and more than doubled its net income. Analysts expect its 2026 revenue to nearly quadruple, then climb another 60% in 2027. Micron’s fiscal 2026, which ended in early September, was even wilder. Revenue climbed to $133.2 billion from $37.4 billion, gross margin rose to 80.7% from 39.8%, and net income jumped from about $8.5 billion to roughly $85 billion. Analysts see Micron’s sales roughly doubling again in fiscal 2027 before YoY growth drops to around 16% in fiscal 2028.

Sun sees that expected slowdown as the reason investors still value the pair like boom-and-bust chip stocks instead of paying up for AI growth. SK Hynix’s U.S.-listed shares trade at about 3 times forward earnings, and Micron at around 4.5 times. The investor also points to pressures from outside the industry. Inflation and high interest rates could cool AI spending and leave smaller neocloud companies struggling to build out. And the Democrats’ midterm wins earlier this month put new governors in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, three big data center states, who campaigned on tougher rules for data center construction.

None of that changes the long-term picture much for Sun. Both stocks are “growing like weeds,” but Sun ultimately comes down in favor of one over the other. “If I had to pick one over the other, I’d stick with SK Hynix instead of Micron for three simple reasons: it’s larger, it’s growing faster, and it will remain the market leader in HBM chips,” the 5-star investor summed up.
